tactics.cpn_notes: Counter-surveillance is increasingly informed by cheap technical aids — RF and camera-detector apps, published guard-schedule leaks, review-site and social posts revealing plainclothes patterns, and mapping tools used to plan surveillance-detection routes — that let an actor characterize a facility's observation coverage before committing to an approach.

credibility.criteria: Credibility rises with corroboration across modalities, persistence over time, and recoverable evidence that the actor is probing or defeating the facility's observation of the actor rather than merely present near the site. Credibility falls when the source, the content, or the temporal pattern is thin, and when a plausible legitimate reason for the evasive or testing behavior was never ruled out.
high_signal_anchors: Cross-modal corroboration — a guard-reaction test on camera, a staff account of a staged distraction, and repeated approach variation against the same facility within overlapping timeframes.
Temporal persistence — counter-surveillance behavior observed across multiple visits over weeks, not a single evasive moment.
Material evidence — recovered notes on camera positions and blind spots, guard-timing logs kept by the actor, RF- or camera-detector tools, or route sketches for defeating coverage of the site.
First-hand witness fidelity — a named guard or officer who watched the actor test a reaction and then withdraw; high-resolution reporting of the stimulus, the response measured, and the timing.
Behavioral specificity — the actor's evasion is keyed to this facility's specific cameras, patrol pattern, or plainclothes coverage rather than generic caution.
Source motivation aligned with accuracy — trained security observer reporting through a formal channel, not an informal tip with a competing agenda.
low_signal_anchors: Source-quality weakness — single anonymous tip, reporter cannot be re-contacted to confirm the evasive behavior.
Content-specificity weakness — vague 'seemed to be checking the cameras' with no described act that distinguishes probing from ordinary glancing.
Temporal-pattern weakness — one apparently evasive moment with no follow-through or repetition.
Source-motivation misalignment — reporter has a structural reason to embellish (prior dispute with the person, tenant rivalry, litigation).

Unrebutted legitimate explanation — the testing or evasive behavior admits a benign reading (privacy-conscious member of the public, journalist, process server, someone avoiding an ex) that investigation did not exclude.
Reconstructive memory — reporting delay long enough that ordinary movement is retrofitted into a counter-surveillance narrative.

capability.criteria: Capability rises when the actor's counter-surveillance shows operational discipline — accurate reading of camera coverage, correct inference of plainclothes and patrol patterns, controlled testing of guard reaction, and movement designed to defeat pattern-detection and following. Capability falls with clumsy, self-defeating evasion, reliance on public rumor about coverage, and probing that immediately exposes the actor.
high_signal_anchors: Accurate coverage reading — the actor correctly identifies real camera fields, blind spots, and which personnel are plainclothes, demonstrating trained observation of the observers.

Controlled reaction testing — a staged stimulus (dropped package, briefly triggered door, staged distraction) executed to measure response time and posture, then a clean withdrawal without committing.
Surveillance-detection movement — the actor runs a route or timing pattern designed to reveal and shake following coverage, indicating knowledge of surveillance-detection tradecraft.
Counter-pattern discipline — the actor deliberately varies approach, dress, vehicle, and timing across visits to deny the facility a stable pattern-of-life to detect.
Technical-aid literacy — the actor uses RF or camera detectors, signal-mapping, or coverage research productively rather than as props.
Cut-out and exposure control — the actor uses intermediaries, avoids a consistent return signature, and manages what any single camera or officer can attribute to the actor.
low_signal_anchors: Self-defeating evasion — theatrical dodging that draws more attention than a normal approach would.
Rumor-only coverage knowledge — everything the actor 'knows' about cameras and guards is public gossip or review-site posts, with no verified operational reach.
Probe exposed on first attempt — the reaction test immediately identified the actor as the source of the stimulus.
No-concealment repetition — repeated testing with the same appearance, vehicle, and timing, defeating the purpose of counter-surveillance.
Misreads coverage — the actor fixates on decoy or non-functional cameras and misses live coverage, showing poor tradecraft.
Direct-contact breach — the actor asked staff directly about camera or guard coverage, surrendering the concealment counter-surveillance is meant to preserve.

intent.criteria: Intent rises when counter-surveillance progresses from casual caution toward deliberate, repeated defeat of the facility's observation, when the actor retains what was learned about coverage, and when the evasion is paired with stated hostility toward the site or with other target-development behavior. Intent falls with generic privacy caution, isolated evasive moments, and a verifiable benign purpose.
high_signal_anchors: Behavioral progression casual-to-deliberate — an observable shift from ordinary caution to systematic probing and defeat of the site's coverage.
Facility-specific counter-surveillance — the effort concentrates on this site's cameras, guards, and following coverage rather than general situational awareness anywhere.
Operational specificity in testing — the actor measures response time, identifies who responds, or maps exactly which fields capture the actor, treating the answers as inputs to an approach.
Sustained adaptation to defender posture — the actor tracks changes in the facility's coverage over time and re-routes or re-times to stay unseen.
Retention of what was learned — coverage maps, guard-timing notes, or annotated imagery of camera positions kept and organized, suggesting later operational use.

Hostile attribution paired with counter-surveillance — the actor has expressed grievance toward the facility AND is observed defeating its observation of the actor; the combination is intent-diagnostic in a way no single indicator captures.
low_signal_anchors: Generic privacy caution — broad wariness of cameras consistent with an ordinary privacy-conscious person, not pinned to this site as an objective.
One-time evasion without escalation — a single evasive moment that did not repeat or develop.
Verifiable legitimate purpose — journalist, licensed investigator, process server, or someone avoiding a personal contact surfaces and checks out.
No retention behavior — coverage noticed in passing but nothing recorded, mapped, or organized.
Target ambiguity — evasive behavior spread across many locations without narrowing counter-surveillance to this facility.

opportunity.criteria: Opportunity rises when the actor can act on knowledge of the facility's observation — combining a working model of camera coverage and patrol timing, a demonstrated ability to move unseen, exploited insider knowledge of the security picture, and positional presence during low-coverage windows. Opportunity falls with observation the actor cannot defeat, distance not closed, or a covert posture the actor has not detected; when opportunity appears reduced, the durability of that reduction matters.
high_signal_anchors: No detection friction encountered — the actor moves against the site repeatedly without being reliably observed, recorded attributable, or followed.

Coverage-timing mastery — the actor reliably knows when cameras are unmonitored, when patrols are thin, and which windows minimize the site's observation of the actor. The informational dimension of opportunity.
Blind-spot and following knowledge — the actor knows camera dead zones, patrol gaps, and how to break any following coverage around the facility.

Insider connection being exploited — an identified employee, contractor, or vendor relationship the actor is actively leveraging for the security-coverage picture. Dormant connections are potential, not realized; the exploitation pattern is what is high-signal.
Geographic-temporal proximity — the actor lives or works near the facility and is present during its low-coverage windows.
Unseen access achieved — the actor has moved through the site or its approaches without generating attributable coverage.
low_signal_anchors: Covert coverage undetected by the actor — the facility's discreet or plainclothes observation is capturing the actor without the actor's awareness. Durable signal: sticky unless the actor detects and adapts to it.
Institutional rule-out of insider access — access audits or process actively cleared the possibility the actor is drawing on inside knowledge of the security picture.
Structural access degradation — the actor's prior source of coverage knowledge terminated (role ended, contract lapsed, relocation).
Detection friction encountered without adaptation — the actor was observed and challenged, left, and did not return or change method. Transient: may flip if the actor adapts.
Geographic distance not closed — the actor is remote and defeating the site's coverage in person requires a travel investment not yet made.
Posture change created barriers — new or randomized coverage, covert overlays, or active surveillance-detection countermeasures block the actor's known evasion methods; transient unless sustained.

false_positive_context.criteria: Many legitimate activities resemble surveillance detection on the surface — a privacy-conscious member of the public avoiding cameras looks similar to an actor mapping coverage; a journalist or licensed investigator working discreetly looks similar to counter-surveillance. What distinguishes a false positive is whether the underlying behavior has a verifiable legitimate purpose, a transparent identity behind it, or institutional accountability that can be checked.
contexts: Verified professional purpose — authorized security consultants and red-teamers conducting sanctioned surveillance-detection or penetration testing of the facility; auditors verifying camera and guard coverage under contract.
Legal authority — authorized law-enforcement counter-surveillance and covert operations; licensed private investigators working lawful matters discreetly; process servers avoiding avoidance.
Privacy-conscious public — ordinary people who dislike being filmed, avoid cameras, or take indirect routes for personal-safety or privacy reasons unrelated to the site.
Press and research activity — journalists protecting sources or working sensitively near a facility; academics studying surveillance or urban movement.
Personal-safety avoidance — individuals evading an abuser, stalker, or personal contact whose movements coincidentally read as counter-surveillance near the facility.

assessment_guidance.threshold_guidance: Findings correlating with staging-class facility behaviors elsewhere — accelerant or explosive-precursor acquisition, observed dry runs against the site, emplacement of materiel, or alignment with an occupancy or anniversary window — warrant immediate activation of response protocols regardless of this tactic's internal tier. Tier-determination for this tactic's findings depends on three factors: credibility of the indicator, breadth across modalities, and persistence over time. A single low-credibility indicator with an available legitimate explanation (privacy-conscious member of the public) sits at the monitoring tier. A single high-credibility indicator with operational specificity — a measured guard-reaction test or a deliberate route to defeat following coverage of this facility — sits at the investigation tier. Because counter-surveillance is deliberately covert, its low detectability should raise, not lower, analytic weight: absence of an obvious signal is consistent with disciplined tradecraft, not with absence of threat. Cross-modal corroboration — grievance plus coverage-mapping plus reaction-testing against the same site — sits at the elevation tier and warrants treating as coordinated facility target development by a disciplined actor. Indicators persisting despite implemented countermeasures, or evidence the actor has detected and adapted to covert coverage, sit at the committed-actor tier, suggesting potential entry into mobilization. Multiple lower-priority indicators correlating temporally or modally may compose to a higher aggregate tier than any single finding warrants; consumer triage tooling should make this composition rule explicit. Tier-triggered actions: monitoring triggers discreet logging and pattern-detection; investigation triggers actor-identification and a facility coverage-gap review; elevation triggers covert-coverage reinforcement and countermeasure activation appropriate to the site's posture; the committed-actor tier triggers a defensive-posture upgrade held as close-hold to avoid confirming coverage to the actor; a confirmed actor matching a known threat-actor profile at any tier warrants urgent law-enforcement coordination.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor tests guard or officer reaction to a staged stimulus — a dropped package, a briefly triggered door or alarm, a staged distraction — to measure response time and posture, then withdraws without committing
Threat actor runs decoy or dry-approach passes at the facility to see who responds, flushing plainclothes, roving, or covert security into the open

Threat actor works to identify and map the facility's coverage of the actor — spotting CCTV fields that capture the actor, picking out plainclothes or roving personnel, and noting which positions can see or record the actor
Threat actor deliberately varies approach, appearance, vehicle, and timing across visits to defeat the facility's pattern-of-life detection and deny security a stable baseline

Threat actor detects and evades being followed or observed by facility security or law enforcement — running surveillance-detection routes, using cut-outs, and controlling exposure to break any coverage of the actor

countermeasures.measure: Train guards and officers to recognize counter-surveillance behavior directed at them — reaction-tests, decoy passes, coverage-mapping, and approach variation — and to report it discreetly rather than reacting in a way that confirms coverage to the actor
countermeasures.limitations: Depends on observer discipline and turnover; disciplined actors deliberately keep each probe below the threshold any single guard would flag, and reporting culture varies by site

countermeasures.measure: Maintain covert and plainclothes observation overlays and concealed CCTV so the facility's coverage of an approaching actor is not itself observable, denying counter-surveillance the confirmation it seeks
countermeasures.limitations: Covert coverage is expensive to sustain and degrades once patterns leak; a disciplined actor running surveillance-detection routes may still detect and adapt to it over repeated visits

countermeasures.measure: Randomize patrol timing, routes, and response choreography so the actor cannot build a stable baseline to probe, and so a reaction-test yields no reliable model of the site's posture
countermeasures.limitations: Randomization trades efficiency for unpredictability and can degrade coverage of fixed critical points; determined actors compensate by sampling across more visits

countermeasures.measure: Log and correlate anomalous test-class events across the site — false alarms, dropped-package reports, brief unexplained door triggers, and repeat visitors observed watching the guard response — into a suspicious-activity pipeline that surfaces probing patterns
countermeasures.limitations: Test events individually resemble routine nuisance incidents; correlation requires disciplined logging and analytic capacity many facilities lack, and closed or oblique probing may never enter the pipeline

response_protocols.trigger: Counter-surveillance behavior reported against the facility — a guard-reaction test, a decoy or dry-approach pass, observed coverage-mapping, or an actor watching who responds to a stimulus
response_protocols.action: Open or update the facility threat case without tipping the actor. Conduct a 24-hour preliminary assessment: (a) discreetly corroborate the observation across CCTV and guard accounts, (b) preserve imagery and logs of the testing behavior, (c) review whether covert coverage captured the actor, (d) brief facility security leadership close-hold and avoid overt posture changes that confirm coverage. Document all sourcing.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Actor identified with apparent means and proximity, OR the actor is observed detecting and adapting to covert coverage, OR indicators across other facility tactics surface for the same actor
response_protocols.legal_notes: Covert observation and any monitoring of an identified actor may implicate privacy, anti-stalking, and wiretap statutes that vary by jurisdiction. Consult counsel before active or covert monitoring; document the investigative basis for any action.

response_protocols.trigger: Confirmed disciplined counter-surveillance by an identified actor — surveillance-detection routes, use of cut-outs, or evidence the actor has detected and is defeating the site's coverage
response_protocols.action: Treat as an advanced-tradecraft indicator and elevate. Reinforce covert coverage held close-hold, coordinate with law enforcement on discreet follow, avoid revealing the full security picture, and reassess the facility's coverage gaps the actor may be exploiting. Hold posture changes as close-hold to prevent confirming coverage to the actor.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Counter-surveillance resolves to a specific actor with staging-class behavior elsewhere, or a date-certain threat emerges
response_protocols.legal_notes: Coordinated covert surveillance and law-enforcement follow raise heightened legal exposure; document the threat basis, defend proportionality, and keep counsel engaged throughout.

tactics.field_notes: Surveillance detection is the actor turning the lens around — not watching the building, but watching whether the building is watching the actor. The clearest tells are small and easy to dismiss one at a time: a package dropped near an entrance to see how fast a guard moves, a first pass that seems to accomplish nothing but flushes a plainclothes officer into view, the same person arriving three times looking different each time. Because good counter-surveillance is designed to be invisible, the absence of an obvious signal is not reassurance — it is consistent with discipline. The practitioner error is reacting visibly to a probe, which hands the actor exactly the reaction they staged the test to measure. The right posture is discreet: log it, preserve it, keep covert coverage covert, and let the pattern assemble before the actor knows they have been seen.
observed_contexts: actor who dropped a bag near a lobby entrance and timed the guard response on two separate visits before withdrawing each time
repeat visitor who changed vehicles and clothing across approaches, defeating the guard force's ability to recognize a pattern until CCTV review connected the visits
case where an actor's first pass at a facility drew a plainclothes officer into the open, after which the actor never returned by the same route
[literature: SANDIA-GARCIA-VAPPS-2006 / DHS-ISC-RMP-2021 pattern — adversary reaction-testing and coverage-mapping of a facility's protection system before an approach]

facility.scope: Tactics centered on a physical venue, structure, or built environment as the primary target. The adversary's primary objective is damage, destruction, denial, or symbolic action against the place itself. Incidental human harm in an unoccupied facility does not move the tactic to People.

organization.scope: Tactics centered on an institution, mission, brand, or operational continuity as the primary target. The adversary's primary objective is disruption, delegitimization, infiltration, or coercion of what the organization does or represents, distinct from its facilities or its individuals.

infrastructure.scope: Tactics centered on infrastructure or technical systems as the primary target. The adversary's primary objective is disruption, degradation, or compromise of the system's function — physical infrastructure, cyber-physical systems, or critical service delivery. Cyber-Physical Nexus tactics are tagged via the cpn field on tactic.

actor_profiles.name: Fixated Individual
actor_profiles.description: Psychologically-driven actor with obsessive focus on a specific named target. The fixation is the defining characteristic — this actor's threat is organized entirely around one person. Motivation is personal, delusional, or grievance-rooted. Follows a slow-building predatory pathway that may span months to years. Clinical anchor: WAVR-21, PATH model, Threat Assessment in Schools.
behavioral_markers: Sustained surveillance or contact attempts directed at one specific named target
Leakage of fixation content to third parties — friends, family, online platforms
Escalating attempts to communicate with or approach the target despite rejection
Acquisition of the target's personal information, schedule, and location patterns
Grievance documentation — letters, journals, social media posts referencing the target

actor_profiles.name: Domestic / Intimate Partner
actor_profiles.description: Actor in or formerly in an intimate, family, or cohabiting relationship with the target. The prior relationship is both the access vector and the motivational anchor. Distinct from the Fixated Individual — the pathway is rooted in control, jealousy, or retaliation rather than obsessive attachment from a distance. Covers intimate partner violence, domestic homicide, stalking by former partners, and family-based violence.
behavioral_markers: Prior or current intimate/family relationship with the target
History of controlling, coercive, or threatening behavior within the relationship
Violation of protective or restraining orders
Monitoring of target's location, communications, and social relationships
Escalation following separation, divorce proceedings, or custody disputes

actor_profiles.name: Crisis-Driven
actor_profiles.description: Individual actor whose pathway to violence is precipitated by an identifiable personal crisis — job loss, financial ruin, relationship breakdown, mental health episode, or a desire for notoriety and legacy. Unlike the Fixated Individual, the target is often symbolic or opportunistic rather than a specific named person. The crisis compresses Phase 1 dramatically: the window from ideation to action may be days or weeks, not months. The notoriety-seeking dimension connects this actor type to attribution-seeking Phase 4 behavior even without ideological content.
behavioral_markers: Identifiable precipitating crisis event immediately preceding behavioral change
Rapid deterioration in work performance, relationships, or personal stability
Leakage of intent — often to multiple people, sometimes publicly
Language expressing desire to be known, remembered, or understood
Target selection based on symbolic representation of the grievance source, not personal relationship

actor_profiles.name: Malicious Insider
actor_profiles.description: Current employee, contractor, or trusted-access holder who deliberately exploits their legitimate access to harm the organization, its people, or its assets. The trust relationship is the attack surface. Motivation may be grievance-based, financially motivated, or ideological. Phase 1 is compressed because the actor is already inside — they know the target, the layout, the security gaps, and the personnel.
behavioral_markers: Observable behavioral deterioration — withdrawal, hostility, policy violations
Anomalous access patterns — systems, locations, or data outside their operational need
Unexplained external contact establishment or suspicious external relationships
Acquisition of materials inconsistent with job role (portable storage, recording equipment)
Testing organizational response to minor violations to calibrate detection capability

actor_profiles.name: Coerced Insider
actor_profiles.description: Current trusted-access holder who is being blackmailed, threatened, or otherwise coerced into facilitating an attack or intelligence collection operation. The actor knows what they are doing but is not acting freely. Coercion may be based on personal compromising information, threats to family, or financial leverage. Detection is complicated because the actor's outward grievance indicators are suppressed — they appear compliant rather than hostile.
behavioral_markers: Sudden behavioral change without apparent internal grievance — anxiety, hypervigilance, social withdrawal
Unexplained financial pressure or sudden resolution of financial problems
Unusual communications security behaviors — new devices, encrypted apps, changed routines
Compliance with unusual external requests without pushback or documentation
Reluctance to discuss personal life; possible indicators of external surveillance of the actor themselves

actor_profiles.name: Recruited Insider
actor_profiles.description: Current trusted-access holder who has been deliberately recruited by an external actor — typically a state intelligence service, organized criminal group, or competitor — and is willingly cooperating. Unlike the coerced insider, this actor chose the relationship. They are disciplined, operationally patient, and actively work to expand their access and preserve their position. Among the hardest insider threat profiles to detect.
behavioral_markers: Sustained covert relationship with an external handler, often disguised as a professional or personal contact
Deliberate access scope expansion beyond their operational role over time
Disciplined information aggregation across systems and people without triggering individual alarms
Unexplained affluence or financial activity inconsistent with salary
High operational security — carefully manages evidence trail, may generate false audit records

actor_profiles.name: Negligent Insider
actor_profiles.description: Current trusted-access holder who creates risk through carelessness, poor security hygiene, or disregard for policy — without intent to cause harm. Not a threat actor in the traditional sense, but a significant risk vector. The negligent insider is frequently the entry point exploited by external actors. Susceptibility to social engineering and phishing is the primary mechanism.
behavioral_markers: Repeated security policy violations without apparent concern for consequences
Susceptibility to social engineering attempts — shares passwords, follows unauthorized instructions
Ignores escalating warning signals or security notifications
Uses personal devices or unsecured channels for sensitive work
Does not report suspicious contacts or requests from unknown parties

actor_profiles.name: Unwitting Insider
actor_profiles.description: Current trusted-access holder who is being exploited by an external actor without their knowledge. Their normal work behavior is the delivery mechanism. They may provide access, information, or physical proximity that they believe is routine. Detection requires identifying the external actor doing the exploiting — the insider's behavior appears normal because it is normal from their perspective. A state intelligence service using a foreign business contact as an unwitting collection platform is the archetype.
behavioral_markers: From the insider's perspective: normal behavior — no behavioral indicators present
Detection pathway: identify the external actor, then map who they have access to
May be approached under a professional or personal pretext with no indication of intelligence purpose
The exploiting actor manages the relationship to keep the insider unaware
Post-detection: insider is typically a victim/witness, not a prosecutorial target

actor_profiles.name: Opportunistic Criminal
actor_profiles.description: Financially motivated actor with minimal planning who exploits available opportunity. Target is selected based on perceived vulnerability, not advance research. Low operational sophistication and low operational security — evidence trail is typically recoverable. Violence is instrumental and proportional to perceived resistance. Acts quickly on available conditions rather than waiting for optimal timing.
behavioral_markers: Target selection based on visible vulnerability — unlocked vehicle, isolated pedestrian, unattended property
Minimal pre-attack preparation or reconnaissance
Low operational security — no counter-surveillance behavior
Improvised capability — uses whatever is at hand
Pattern of escalation from minor offenses toward more serious crimes

actor_profiles.name: Professional Criminal
actor_profiles.description: Financially motivated actor operating as a hired professional — assassin, kidnap-for-ransom specialist, security contractor operating outside legal bounds. Executes for payment, not ideology. Applies professional tradecraft: pre-operational surveillance, covert capability acquisition, practiced withdrawal. Full phase completion is the operational norm. Distinguishable from organized criminal enterprise by individual or small-team structure and contract-based operation.
behavioral_markers: Pre-operational surveillance of target using professional counter-detection methods
Covert capability acquisition through channels that obscure the procurement trail
No ideological or personal connection to the target — purely transactional
Systematic withdrawal and evidence management post-operation
Financial transaction pattern consistent with contracted payment receipt

actor_profiles.name: Organized Criminal Group
actor_profiles.description: Enterprise-level criminal organization with division of roles, financial infrastructure, and operational capacity spanning multiple operations. Cartel, syndicate, or organized crime network. Kidnap-for-ransom, extortion, trafficking, and targeted violence against rivals or witnesses are primary THREAT-relevant operations. Uses cutouts, intermediaries, and financial layering. Phase 4 Financial Disposition is a defining operational capability.
behavioral_markers: Multiple actors with compartmented and specialized roles
Financial infrastructure for receiving and laundering proceeds
Use of cutouts and intermediaries to separate principals from operations
Established communications security and counter-surveillance protocols
Pattern of prior incidents establishing organizational TTPs

actor_profiles.name: Corporate Spy
actor_profiles.description: Actor focused on covert intelligence collection — stealing trade secrets, IP, client data, strategic plans, or personnel information for delivery to a competitor, state actor, or criminal purchaser. The defining operational logic is preservation of access: unlike the saboteur, the corporate spy wants to keep going back. Stealth and access maintenance are primary operational values. May be an insider acting on behalf of an external principal or an external actor who has gained insider access through recruitment or social engineering.
behavioral_markers: Covert access to sensitive data or systems beyond their operational role
Aggregation of information across multiple systems and people in a pattern inconsistent with job function
Deliberate concealment of information collection activities — after-hours access, personal devices
Sustained contact with an external handler disguised as professional or personal relationship
Deliberate preservation of access — avoids triggering reviews, maintains low profile

actor_profiles.name: Industrial Saboteur
actor_profiles.description: Actor focused on physically destroying or disabling operational capability — machinery, production systems, infrastructure, or records. Unlike the corporate spy, the saboteur's operation is consumptive: the objective is to break something, not take something. May be grievance-driven, state-directed, competitor-directed, or ideologically motivated. Timing around business-critical events (product launch, merger, regulatory deadline) is a characteristic indicator. Uses legitimate access to reach systems that would otherwise require forced entry.
behavioral_markers: Access to operational or physical systems beyond normal job function
Unexplained presence near critical equipment, infrastructure nodes, or safety systems
Evidence of tampering with machinery, processes, or safety controls
Timing correlation with business-critical events or organizational stress periods
May disguise access as maintenance, inspection, or contractor activity

actor_profiles.name: Issue-Oriented Activist
actor_profiles.description: Ideologically motivated actor whose goal is exposure, embarrassment, disruption, or policy change — not physical harm to people. Physical harm to persons is actively avoided because it would undermine the message. Property damage and operational disruption are within scope. Attribution is essential — the claim is the point. Operates in a legal-to-illegal spectrum that makes early intervention difficult. Distinguishable from terrorist by the absence of mass casualty intent and the communicative primacy of the non-violent message.
behavioral_markers: Public organizing activity, social media coordination, and recruitment visible before the action
Targets selected for symbolic or operational significance to the cause, not for maximum casualties
Prior incidents of civil disobedience or low-level property disruption in the pattern
Strong attribution-seeking behavior — prepared statements, media contacts, livestreaming
Avoidance of methods likely to cause human casualties

actor_profiles.name: Saboteur
actor_profiles.description: Ideologically motivated actor whose goal is the destruction or disabling of infrastructure or operational capability. Physical harm to people is acceptable, not the primary objective. Targets are selected for their operational significance — pipelines, power nodes, water systems, communications infrastructure. May operate as a lone actor or in a small cell. Attribution is conditional: environmental or anti-state saboteurs may claim credit; state-affiliated saboteurs typically do not.
behavioral_markers: Reconnaissance of infrastructure targets — substations, pipelines, pumping stations, communication towers
Acquisition of destructive materials — explosives, incendiaries, or tools for physical tampering
Operational security behaviors suggesting awareness of surveillance
Target selection pattern focused on operational chokepoints and high-consequence nodes
May conduct Partial Approach Rehearsal at target sites across multiple days

actor_profiles.name: Terrorist
actor_profiles.description: Ideologically or politically motivated actor who uses violence as a communicative instrument — to coerce policy, shape public perception, or demonstrate capability. The violence is not the end; it is the message. Attribution is operationally required: terrorism without a claim loses its coercive power. Target selection is based on symbolic value or policy leverage, not maximum casualty efficiency. Organized cells apply full phase completion. Lone terrorists may compress Phase 1 based on radicalization timeline.
behavioral_markers: Ideological radicalization indicators — consumption of extremist content, rhetoric escalation, community withdrawal
Operational security behaviors — encrypted communications, new devices, changed routines
Target selection research focused on symbolic value or media visibility
Capability acquisition for mass-casualty or high-impact methods
Phase 4 attribution is mandatory — prepared communiqués, media contacts, or symbolic claim delivery

actor_profiles.name: Violent Extremist
actor_profiles.description: Ideologically motivated actor for whom causing mass harm or death is the operational end, not merely the instrument. Distinct from the terrorist — coercion is not the goal; elimination or destruction of the target group is. Attribution may be claimed or implicit but is not operationally required. Mass casualty capacity is the capability selection criterion. May exhibit martyrdom posture in Phase 4 — no evasion planning, active engagement with responders, or suicide by cop.
behavioral_markers: Escalating dehumanization of a target group in communications and expressed ideology
Leakage of eliminationist language — destruction, annihilation, cleansing rhetoric
Acquisition of mass-casualty capable methods — firearms, explosives, vehicles
Target selection based on demographic density of the target group, not symbolic value
Martyrdom posture — no withdrawal planning, final communications framed as legacy

actor_profiles.name: State Actor
actor_profiles.description: Nation-state directed, sponsored, or sanctioned adversary operating with the full intelligence apparatus of a state — collection, planning support, logistics, and exfiltration infrastructure. Deniability architecture is a Phase 1 planning input, not an afterthought. Highest capability across all matrices. May use proxy actors. Operations span all four matrices simultaneously for complex targets. Full phase completion is the norm; Phase 1 may extend over months with parallel Phase 2 preparation.
behavioral_markers: Professional counter-surveillance and surveillance detection routines throughout all phases
Multi-actor team with compartmented roles and need-to-know discipline
Access to sophisticated capability — specialized tools, forged documents, sterile communications
Pre-planned withdrawal with assets positioned before operation initiation
Deniability architecture visible in how the operation is structured and what is left behind

actor_profiles.name: State-Sponsored Actor
actor_profiles.description: Actor funded, directed, or enabled by a state intelligence service while maintaining a non-state appearance — contractor, criminal organization, hacktivist front, or private intelligence firm operating with state backing. Witting of the state relationship. The sponsoring state gains operational capability with plausible deniability. Distinct from State Actor (direct operation) — the sponsoring relationship adds a layer that complicates attribution and legal accountability.
behavioral_markers: Operates with resources and capability inconsistent with apparent organizational size or revenue
Access to state-grade intelligence products and tradecraft without apparent state affiliation
Operations align with sponsoring state's geopolitical interests or target lists
Financial flows from obscured state-affiliated sources
Counter-attribution behaviors designed to point to non-state actors

actor_profiles.name: Unwitting State Proxy
actor_profiles.description: An individual or organization exploited by a state intelligence service as an access or collection vehicle without their knowledge. Recruited under a false pretext — as a researcher, business contact, journalist, or academic — and used to provide physical access, information, or relationships that the state actor cannot reach directly. From the proxy's perspective, the relationship is entirely normal. Detection requires identifying the state handler and mapping who they have cultivated access to. The proxy is typically a victim, not a prosecutorial target.
behavioral_markers: From the proxy's perspective: entirely normal behavior — no meaningful behavioral indicators
Detection pathway: identify the state handler's relationship network, not the proxy's behavior
May have been approached with flattery, professional opportunity, or apparent friendship
Provides access or information to the handler believing it serves a legitimate purpose
Relationship managed by the handler to maintain the proxy's unawareness and continued cooperation

actor_profiles.name: State-Directed Corporate Front
actor_profiles.description: A commercial entity — business, research institution, joint venture, or consultancy — that operates as a vehicle for state intelligence collection or influence operations. Leadership is witting; operational staff may range from witting to entirely unwitting. The commercial cover provides access to sensitive environments that direct state actors cannot reach. Detection requires analysis of the corporate structure, beneficial ownership, and the pattern of access sought rather than behavioral indicators in individual personnel.
behavioral_markers: Corporate structure with beneficial ownership obscured through multiple jurisdictions
Business activities that create access to sensitive technology, infrastructure, or personnel
Employees who seek unusually broad access beyond their stated commercial purpose
Partnerships or contracts that provide physical or network access to protected environments
Pattern of interest in sensitive information inconsistent with stated commercial objectives

actor_profiles.name: Transnational Criminal Organization
actor_profiles.description: Formal criminal organization operating across national borders with quasi-state capabilities. Conducts kidnapping-for-ransom, assassination, extortion, smuggling, and corruption of government officials at scale. Includes cartels, transnational gangs, and criminal networks with documented convergence with state and terrorist actors. Characterized by territorial control, paramilitary units, and sophisticated operational security.
behavioral_markers: Surveillance and pattern-of-life collection on target consistent with professional operational planning
Use of cutouts, intermediaries, and encrypted communications to insulate principals
Multiple operational actors with defined roles — intelligence, logistics, execution
Cross-border financial flows and money laundering infrastructure
Willingness to conduct violence against witnesses, family members, or security personnel

actor_profiles.name: Contract Killer
actor_profiles.description: Individual engaged to commit murder in exchange for payment. May be employed by organized criminal groups, transnational criminal organizations, state actors, commercial actors, or private individuals. Professional execution and operational security distinguish this actor from impulsive criminal violence. The transactional nature means the actor has no personal grievance — threat does not de-escalate if the underlying grievance is resolved.
behavioral_markers: Methodical pre-attack surveillance and target confirmation behaviors
Use of counter-surveillance techniques and route variation during reconnaissance
Acquisition of weapons through channels designed to prevent attribution
Limited digital footprint and use of cash or cryptocurrency for operational expenses
No observable personal grievance with the target — access to target is the only objective

actor_profiles.name: Abductor
actor_profiles.description: Actor who takes a person by force, deception, or coercion for purposes of ransom, coercion, exploitation, or use as leverage against a third party. May operate independently or as a member of an organized group. Kidnapping-for-ransom operations involve sustained engagement with victim and family or organization over time. Coercive abduction may be used to extract access credentials, information, or compliance from the victim or a connected party.
behavioral_markers: Extended pattern-of-life collection to identify predictable routines and low-coverage windows
Acquisition of restraints, vehicles, or communications equipment inconsistent with known activities
Probing of security measures — testing response times, guard schedules, or escort procedures
Pre-positioning of resources at likely intercept points along target's regular routes
Establishment of secure holding location prior to execution

actor_profiles.name: Extortionist
actor_profiles.description: Actor who uses threatened harm — to a person, their family, their assets, or their reputation — to compel payment or behavioral compliance. May leverage compromising information, physical threats, or harm to third parties as leverage. Distinct from kidnapping in that the primary tool is the threat rather than the act. Threat may be sustained over extended periods and escalated incrementally to maximize compliance.
behavioral_markers: Initial contact establishing the threat and demand, often through anonymous or obfuscated channels
Demonstrated access to private information or ability to harm as proof of capability
Escalating contact frequency or threatened consequence when demands are not met
Monitoring of target's public communications and security posture for signs of law enforcement contact
Use of cryptocurrency or structured financial channels to receive payment without attribution

actor_profiles.name: Service User
actor_profiles.description: Individual who has a legitimate service relationship with the target organization — patient, client, student, customer — and directs violence or threatening behavior toward staff or other service users within that context. The highest-volume category of workplace violence in the United States (Cal/OSHA Type II). Threat typically emerges from dissatisfaction with service, denial of benefits, or perceived mistreatment. Violence is often impulsive and situationally triggered rather than premeditated.
behavioral_markers: Verbal aggression or threatening statements directed at staff during service interactions
Escalating complaints with explicit or implicit threats of harm
History of disruptive behavior across multiple service interactions
Expressed grievance specifically targeting a named staff member or service location
Presence in restricted areas or repeated attempts to access staff outside normal service channels

actor_profiles.name: Aggrieved Group
actor_profiles.description: Organized or semi-organized collective with a shared grievance against a specific organization, its leadership, or its policies. Distinguished from ideological actors (AP015–AP018) by the specificity and personal nature of the grievance — this group was directly affected by a decision, product failure, policy, or perceived injustice. May organize protests, harassment campaigns, coordinated complaints, or escalate to physical disruption and targeted threats against executives or staff.
behavioral_markers: Coordinated contact campaigns — calls, emails, social media — directed at specific staff or leadership
Organized protest activity at organizational facilities or events
Doxing of executive or staff personal information to group members
Explicit threatening communications directed at named individuals
Escalation pattern: public campaign → targeted harassment → physical threat

escalation_rubric.composite_math: Recommended composite is the geometric mean of the four type-level potentials, with detectability flipped to reflect its mitigating role: escalation_weight = (impact_potential × blast_radius_potential × recoverability_inverse × (10 - detectability))^(1/4). The geometric mean ensures the composite is bounded 0.0–10.0 and that a weak value on any single axis pulls the composite down — appropriate for security-intuitive 'weakest-link' reading. Detectability is flipped because high observability by trained personnel reduces (not raises) the realized escalation potential. Consumers may substitute weighted-additive or other variants with documented rationale per CONTRIBUTING.md 'Schema design principles.'

severity_floor_rule.definition: A triage floor layered on the severity math: an indicator whose behavior applies DIRECT PHYSICAL FORCE to a person's body carries severity_band = critical at minimum, regardless of its computed escalation_weight. escalation_weight is unchanged — it remains the true severity computation, so the gradient between a single assault (~4.6) and a mass bombing (~8.7) is preserved — but the triage band for any force against a person is critical. Such indicators carry a `severity_floor` field set to "critical". Rationale: a casualty is critical regardless of scale. The severity math gates the top band on blast_radius (population scope), which would place a single-victim killing at high and reserve critical for mass-casualty events; but for triage, any application of force to a person is a top-priority event. Count is a severity GRADIENT (in escalation_weight), not the critical THRESHOLD. This is a values/triage rule, not a change to the weight formula.
severity_floor_rule.applies_to: Behaviors that directly apply physical force to a person: weapon discharge, vehicle ramming, explosive detonation, physical assault, overpowering or incapacitating personnel, taking physical custody by restraint, forcible extraction, and physical restraint or force against a captive.

blast_radius_guidance.definition: blast_radius_potential encodes TOTAL expected victim scope for the indicator class: intended targets PLUS expected collateral (bystander / non-target) casualties. It is not intended-victim count alone — a single-target attack can carry high blast_radius when its method produces collateral (a bombing that kills one intended target and nearby bystanders scores high, not low). Method sets the type-level base rate below; venue, timing, and crowd density modulate at assessment (instance) time.

method_collateral_base_rates.note: Recommended type-level anchors (0.0-10.0) for the attack method a class embodies or presages. Combine with intended-target scope — a mass-casualty-intended attack raises blast_radius above the collateral base rate — and deviate for sub-type. These are the People matrix; other matrices re-derive.

blast_radius_guidance.authoring_notes: Pre-attack indicators inherit the collateral ceiling of the method they presage (acquiring an explosive takes the explosive base rate). Venue-selection and timing signals are bystander-risk indicators even in target-development and mobilization phases — an approach timed to a crowd event, or a firing position with line-of-sight to a gathering. The People matrix models bystanders as a distinct population in tactic TM0306 (Bystander Management); this axis carries the SEVERITY of that exposure, which TM0306 alone does not. Instance-level venue and crowd-density conditioning belongs in the assessment layer, not the type-level base rate.

collateral_reveal_guidance.principle: Collateral-revealed, the parallel to method-revealed: raise blast_radius above the single-victim / method-base floor only where the BEHAVIOR ITSELF observably reveals a group/population target or a public/crowd venue. Do NOT uplift on mere compatibility with a group target (e.g., a target_identity that merely permits a group) — that over-applies and collapses toward a blanket floor. A behavior against a single individual in an unrevealed venue keeps the floor.

tiers.indiscriminate_or_population_target_reve: mass ceiling 7.0-9.0, combined with the method base rate
tiers.public_or_crowd_venue_revealed: 5.0-7.0 — line-of-sight to a gathering, approach timed to a crowd event, an attack staged in a crowded venue
tiers.bystanders_present_or_managed: 4.0-5.0 — bystander-management behaviors, or occupation/siege of a public site
tiers.cohesive_group_or_affinity_target_reveal: 3.5-4.0 — a specific cohesive group, not a crowd
tiers.single_individual_or_venue_unrevealed: method base rate or single-victim floor (2.5-3.0)

collateral_reveal_guidance.instance_deferral: The statistical likelihood that an unrevealed-venue targeted attack produces bystander casualties is an INSTANCE-level assessment — it depends on the specific target's typical environment (a public figure in crowds vs. a private individual) — and is resolved at assessment time in the instance-conditioning layer, NOT encoded in the type-level blast_radius. Keeping the type-level floor for unrevealed venues is deliberate, not an omission.
collateral_reveal_guidance.computed_critical_requires_both: blast_radius (collateral) alone does not produce a critical band VIA THE COMPUTED WEIGHT. A computed-critical weight requires BOTH mass-lethal impact_potential AND mass blast_radius — the active application or direct acquisition of mass-casualty force. A positioning, timing, or bystander-management behavior with high blast but moderate impact computes to high, not critical. NOTE: this concerns the computed weight only; the separate severity_floor_rule floors any direct-physical-force-on-a-person behavior to critical regardless of computed weight (a casualty is critical at any scale).

blast_radius_guidance.authoring_status: Added rubric v1.1.0 (2026-07-04). Existing scored indicators predate this guidance and still carry single-victim blast_radius (2.5-3.0); re-authoring per this table, and scoring the execution phase, is a pending V1.3 pass (see scoring backlog B-05 / B-09).

escalation_rubric.calibration_guidance: The severity_thresholds above reflect equal-quartile bucketing as the framework's default. Consumers SHOULD calibrate the thresholds to their threat-posture environment for best results. Higher-posture environments (e.g., critical infrastructure, executive protection, dignitary protection) may shift `high` and `critical` thresholds downward (e.g., high=4.0, critical=6.0) to surface medium-weight indicators earlier in triage. Lower-posture environments may shift them upward. Document the rationale for any deviation per CONTRIBUTING.md "Schema design principles".

detection_mesh.principle: THREAT Matrix treats detection and response as a mesh, not a chain. Indicators from any phase, any matrix, and any detection domain can correlate with indicators from anywhere else in the framework. Countermeasures from any domain can compensate for gaps in another. Response protocols from any stakeholder (threat management teams, HR, legal, law enforcement, protective operations, EAP) can fire in parallel on the same indicator set, each acting within their own authority.

axes.name: cross_phase
axes.description: An indicator observed in one phase can correlate to an indicator observed in another phase for the same actor. Late-phase indicators retroactively illuminate earlier-phase activity; early-phase indicators prime recognition of later signals.

axes.name: cross_matrix
axes.description: Adversaries do not respect matrix boundaries. The mesh weaves the four matrices (People, Facilities, Organizations, Infrastructure) into one coherent detection space. An indicator in any matrix can pull context from any other matrix.

axes.name: cross_domain
axes.description: Detection sources are cross-domain: physical observation, CCTV, access logs, social media, peer reports, financial records, IT logs, public records, OSINT. Any domain's signal can activate any phase's detection.

axes.name: cross_countermeasure
axes.description: Countermeasures from any domain can compensate for gaps in another. Defense-in-depth is structural in the framework via the compensates_for links.

axes.name: cross_stakeholder
axes.description: Response protocols fire in parallel, not sequentially. Multiple stakeholders engage the same indicator set from their respective authorities, coordinated via the coordinates_with links.

detection_mesh.doctrinal_antecedent: The structural antecedent is the Kill Web concept in modern military doctrine; THREAT Matrix adapts the principle to physical adversary detection in organizational contexts.

warden_integration.notes: WARDEN alert schema maps to THREAT taxonomy via agentic ingestion pipeline. V3 implementation: WARDEN behavioral alerts to structured TTP assessment in THREAT taxonomy language. Both tools are demonstrably more powerful together: WARDEN detects the pathway; THREAT maps where the actor is in the Threat Lifecycle.

ai_architecture.philosophy: AI is a force multiplier on existing attack vectors — not a separate pathway. AI compresses Phase 1 timelines, lowers tradecraft requirements, and makes capabilities previously requiring nation-state resources accessible to unsophisticated actors. It does not create new physical attack pathways; it reduces the skill floor for existing ones.

vectors.ai_initiated_physical: An autonomous or semi-autonomous AI system directly executes physical harm without real-time human direction at the point of attack. Distinct from cyber_initiated_physical: the attack does not necessarily route through networked cyberspace — the AI agent operates locally, autonomously, in physical space. Examples: AI-directed drones with autonomous targeting, robotic platforms executing without human oversight, compromised autonomous vehicle systems.
vectors.ai_enabled_risks: Capability modifier field on every actor profile. Documents AI-specific risk amplifiers applicable to each actor type. Not a vector — an inventory of how AI tools lower the barrier for existing attack vectors on a per-profile basis.

capability_taxonomy.accelerated_target_research: LLMs, OSINT aggregators, and AI-powered social graph analyzers compress Phase 1 target development from weeks to hours, without requiring technical expertise.
capability_taxonomy.synthetic_identity: AI-generated personas, documents, voice, and online presence used for cover identities, social engineering, or recruitment operations.
capability_taxonomy.deepfake_manipulation: AI-generated audio, video, or text impersonating trusted parties — used for manipulation, extortion, or access enablement.
capability_taxonomy.automated_surveillance: AI-powered monitoring of a target's digital footprint, location patterns, social connections, and behavioral indicators at scale.
capability_taxonomy.autonomous_targeting: AI systems capable of independent targeting decisions for physical harm, without real-time human direction at point of execution.

ai_architecture.cpn_impact: The Cyber-Physical Nexus dimension carries the highest AI amplification risk. AI tools directly accelerate Phase 1 (Target Development) for any actor targeting individuals with a digital footprint. Detection models must account for AI-compressed threat timelines — a Fixated Individual now has access to research capability that previously required professional-grade intelligence resources.
ai_architecture.v2_roadmap: V2 will add per-tactic AI capability annotations, expand ai_enabled_risks with tactic-level associations, and introduce the Operations/scenario composer with AI-assisted behavioral pattern generation.

GULYASH-FIELD-OPS-2004-2026.title: Operational observations: protective intelligence, insider threat, and physical security casework
GULYASH-FIELD-OPS-2004-2026.author: Jay Gulyash
GULYASH-FIELD-OPS-2004-2026.relevance_summary: Pattern documentation synthesized from 15+ years of practitioner work across federal law enforcement, corporate security, and intelligence roles, spanning dozens of domestic and international partner organizations. Tactics, indicators, and countermeasures cited to this source reflect recurring patterns observed in operational practice. Individual cases are not disclosable; the patterns are attestable. Patterns are validated by cross-reference with published threat-assessment literature where possible.

FEIN-VOSSEKUIL-1999.title: Assassination in the United States: An Operational Study of Recent Assassins, Attackers, and Near-Lethal Approachers
FEIN-VOSSEKUIL-1999.author: Fein, R.A. & Vossekuil, B.
FEIN-VOSSEKUIL-1999.relevance_summary: Foundational pathway model for targeted violence: grievance to ideation to research/planning to preparation to breach to attack. Established that violence is a process with observable behavioral stages.

NTAC-MASS-2021.title: Mass Attacks in Public Spaces: 2016-2020
NTAC-MASS-2021.author: U.S. Secret Service, National Threat Assessment Center
NTAC-MASS-2021.relevance_summary: Behavioral analysis of 173 mass attack incidents including pre-attack grievance patterns, communication of intent, target selection factors, and resource acquisition behaviors.

NTAC-SCHOOLS-2019.title: Protecting America's Schools: A U.S. Secret Service Analysis of Targeted School Violence
NTAC-SCHOOLS-2019.author: U.S. Secret Service, National Threat Assessment Center
NTAC-SCHOOLS-2019.relevance_summary: Analysis of targeted school violence incidents documenting social stressors, concerning communications, research on prior attacks, and site-specific planning as pre-attack behavioral indicators.

NTAC-AVERTED-2021.title: Averting Targeted School Violence: A U.S. Secret Service Analysis of Plots Against Schools
NTAC-AVERTED-2021.author: U.S. Secret Service, National Threat Assessment Center
NTAC-AVERTED-2021.relevance_summary: Analysis of averted plots capturing the full Phase 1-2 behavioral arc without execution. Shows what planning and mobilization look like when detected and interrupted.

MELOY-TRAP18-2016.title: The Lone-Actor Terrorist and the TRAP-18
MELOY-TRAP18-2016.author: Meloy, J.R. & Gill, P.
MELOY-TRAP18-2016.relevance_summary: Terrorist Radicalization Assessment Protocol with 8 proximal warning behaviors and 10 distal characteristics, used to assess lone-actor radicalization trajectories.

FBI-PREATTACK-2018.title: A Study of the Pre-Attack Behaviors of Active Shooters in the United States Between 2000 and 2013
FBI-PREATTACK-2018.author: Silver, J., Simons, A., & Craun, S., Federal Bureau of Investigation
FBI-PREATTACK-2018.relevance_summary: Study of 63 active shooters documenting behavioral changes in mental health, interpersonal interactions, leakage, and weapons behaviors in the weeks and months before attacks.

CERT-CSG-7-2022.title: Common Sense Guide to Mitigating Insider Threats, Seventh Edition
CERT-CSG-7-2022.author: Carnegie Mellon University, Software Engineering Institute, CERT Division
CERT-CSG-7-2022.relevance_summary: Comprehensive insider threat mitigation guide based on 1000+ cases. Defines behavioral, digital, psychological, and contextual indicator categories with multi-disciplinary response protocols.

NITTF-GUIDE-2017.title: Insider Threat Guide: A Compendium of Best Practices to Accompany the National Insider Threat Policy and Minimum Standards
NITTF-GUIDE-2017.author: National Insider Threat Task Force (NITTF), ODNI
NITTF-GUIDE-2017.relevance_summary: Federal insider threat program minimum standards including hub/spoke detection model, 5-tier escalation framework (awareness through response), and stakeholder involvement matrix.

ASIS-WVPI-2021.title: ASIS/SHRM WVPI.1-2011 (R2021): Workplace Violence Prevention and Intervention
ASIS-WVPI-2021.author: ASIS International / SHRM
ASIS-WVPI-2021.relevance_summary: ANSI standard defining Threat Assessment Team model, behavioral escalation indicators, 5-level response protocol, and timing windows for workplace violence prevention.

CISA-DIT-2023.title: Defining Insider Threats
CISA-DIT-2023.author: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA)
CISA-DIT-2023.relevance_summary: CISA insider threat definition framework with published behavioral indicator list organized by intentional vs. unintentional categories.

FEIN-VOSSEKUIL-HOLDEN-1995.title: Threat Assessment: An Approach to Prevent Targeted Violence
FEIN-VOSSEKUIL-HOLDEN-1995.author: Fein, R.A., Vossekuil, B., & Holden, G.A.
FEIN-VOSSEKUIL-HOLDEN-1995.relevance_summary: NIJ Research in Action report establishing threat assessment as the preferred approach over threat profiling. Focus on behaviors over traits for targeted violence prevention.

NTAC-SYSTEMS-2020.title: Using a Systems Approach for Threat Assessment Investigations: A 10-Step Guide for Threat Management Professionals
NTAC-SYSTEMS-2020.author: U.S. Secret Service, National Threat Assessment Center
NTAC-SYSTEMS-2020.relevance_summary: Practitioner methodology for systematic threat assessment investigations. 10-step framework for threat management teams applied to organizational settings.

CISA-CONVERGE-2021.title: Convergence of Physical and Cyber Insider Threats
CISA-CONVERGE-2021.author: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA)
CISA-CONVERGE-2021.relevance_summary: Identifies converged physical-cyber insider threat indicators including badge/network anomaly correlation, physical surveillance combined with digital reconnaissance, and cross-domain detection integration.

LLNL-TR-858139.title: Requirements and Recommendations for a Physical Attack Characterization Framework
LLNL-TR-858139.author: McGrath, J.K., Scott, H.R., & Slone, L.R., Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory
LLNL-TR-858139.relevance_summary: DOE/NNSA-sponsored requirements study evaluating whether any existing methodology could serve as a structured framework for characterizing physical adversary action. Concluded existing frameworks are inadequate.

KIM-JONGNAM-KUL-2017.title: Making a Murderer: The Assassination of Kim Jong-nam
KIM-JONGNAM-KUL-2017.author: Lowy Institute (The Interpreter)
KIM-JONGNAM-KUL-2017.relevance_summary: Documents the 13 February 2017 assassination of Kim Jong-nam at Kuala Lumpur International Airport, including the recruitment of two women under a 'prank video for a TV show' media-production cover who applied VX nerve agent without knowing they were committing the assassination. The case is the canonical operational example of bystander recruitment through media-production deception. The Lowy Institute analysis is cited as the operationally focused source; comparable coverage is available from major international news organizations including NPR and CNN.

CHAINALYSIS-CCR-2024.title: Crypto Crime Report — Annual Analysis of Illicit Cryptocurrency Activity
CHAINALYSIS-CCR-2024.author: Chainalysis Inc.
CHAINALYSIS-CCR-2024.relevance_summary: Annual industry report on illicit cryptocurrency flows, ransomware payment patterns, mixing service activity, and the operational characteristics of blockchain-forensics tracing across the cryptocurrency landscape. Cited in TM0405 Financial Disposition where blockchain-forensics tracing capability informs analyst reads on financial-disposition timelines.

START-GTD-2020.title: Global Terrorism Database (GTD)
START-GTD-2020.author: National Consortium for the Study of Terrorism and Responses to Terrorism (START), University of Maryland
START-GTD-2020.relevance_summary: Incident-level database of 200,000+ terrorist events (1970-2020) coded by target type and by nine attack types, including discrete Facility/Infrastructure Attack and Barricade (hostage-taking) categories. Empirical grounding for facility target selection and attack-type distribution.

DHS-ISC-RMP-2021.title: The Risk Management Process for Federal Facilities: An Interagency Security Committee Standard
DHS-ISC-RMP-2021.author: U.S. Department of Homeland Security / CISA Interagency Security Committee (ISC)
DHS-ISC-RMP-2021.relevance_summary: The U.S. government standard for determining Facility Security Levels and selecting baseline physical-security countermeasures for nonmilitary federal facilities. Defines the undesirable-event set (bombing, arson, forced entry, contamination) and the threat/vulnerability/consequence methodology.

SANDIA-RAM-2008.title: Overview of Sandia's Security Risk Assessment Methodologies (SAND2008-1604P)
SANDIA-RAM-2008.author: Jaeger, C.D., Sandia National Laboratories (USDOE/NNSA)
SANDIA-RAM-2008.relevance_summary: Overview of Sandia's family of facility risk-assessment methodologies (RAM-W, RAM-C, and variants) for adversary-path and vulnerability assessment of critical facilities.

SANDIA-GARCIA-DEPPS-2007.title: Design and Evaluation of Physical Protection Systems, 2nd Edition
SANDIA-GARCIA-DEPPS-2007.author: Garcia, M.L., Sandia National Laboratories (Butterworth-Heinemann / Elsevier)
SANDIA-GARCIA-DEPPS-2007.relevance_summary: Foundational text on designing and evaluating facility physical protection systems via detection-delay-response and adversary-sequence path analysis. Methodological backbone for forced-entry and structural-attack delay scoring. ISBN 9780750683524.

SANDIA-GARCIA-VAPPS-2006.title: Vulnerability Assessment of Physical Protection Systems
SANDIA-GARCIA-VAPPS-2006.author: Garcia, M.L., Sandia National Laboratories (Butterworth-Heinemann / Elsevier)
SANDIA-GARCIA-VAPPS-2006.relevance_summary: Sandia's end-to-end vulnerability-assessment process for evaluating how a facility's protection system withstands adversary path and breach scenarios. ISBN 9780750677882.

ATF-EIR-2024.title: United States Bomb Data Center (USBDC) Explosives Incident Report (EIR)
ATF-EIR-2024.author: Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), U.S. Bomb Data Center
ATF-EIR-2024.relevance_summary: Annual national tally of explosions, bombings, device recoveries, suspicious packages, and bomb threats drawn from the Bomb Arson Tracking System (BATS). Direct base rates for IED/VBIED tactics against facilities. Latest edition CY2024.

CISA-BOMBTHREAT-2023.title: Bomb Threat Guide (Version 1.9)
CISA-BOMBTHREAT-2023.author: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Office for Bombing Prevention
CISA-BOMBTHREAT-2023.relevance_summary: Federal operational guidance on bomb-threat assessment, evacuate-vs-shelter decisions, and standoff distances by device size. Informs facility bombing-response protocols and protective measures.

FEMA-426-2011.title: Reference Manual to Mitigate Potential Terrorist Attacks Against Buildings (FEMA-426 / BIPS-06), 2nd Edition
FEMA-426-2011.author: U.S. Department of Homeland Security Science & Technology Directorate / FEMA (Buildings and Infrastructure Protection Series)
FEMA-426-2011.relevance_summary: The definitive U.S. engineering-mitigation reference on blast effects against buildings, standoff distance, progressive-collapse and structural hardening, and a dedicated chemical/biological/radiological (CBR) protection chapter. Multi-domain facility source.

ATF-AIR-2023.title: United States Bomb Data Center (USBDC) Arson Incident Report (AIR), Calendar Year 2023
ATF-AIR-2023.author: Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), U.S. Bomb Data Center
ATF-AIR-2023.relevance_summary: National arson and incendiary-fire incident dataset from BATS, giving structure-fire arson counts, target types, and incendiary methods. Companion to the ATF Explosives Incident Report.

NFPA-INTENTIONAL-2021.title: Intentional Structure Fires
NFPA-INTENTIONAL-2021.author: Campbell, R., National Fire Protection Association (NFPA)
NFPA-INTENTIONAL-2021.relevance_summary: NFPA's statistical analysis of deliberately set structure fires: timing, property-use distribution, area of origin, and casualty/loss patterns. Base rates distinguishing intentional structure fires from accidental.

DOD-UFC4010-2018.title: UFC 4-010-01 DoD Minimum Antiterrorism Standards for Buildings (with Change 3)
DOD-UFC4010-2018.author: U.S. Department of Defense (Unified Facilities Criteria)
DOD-UFC4010-2018.relevance_summary: Mandatory DoD standoff-distance, structural-hardening, and progressive-collapse-avoidance criteria for buildings. The authoritative standard for facility hardening against blast, forced entry, and vehicle attack.

DOD-UFC4022-2017.title: UFC 4-022-01 Security Engineering: Entry Control Facilities / Access Control Points
DOD-UFC4022-2017.author: U.S. Department of Defense (Unified Facilities Criteria)
DOD-UFC4022-2017.relevance_summary: Design criteria for entry-control facilities, active vehicle barriers, and access-point layout to defeat forced or unauthorized entry and vehicle breach at a facility perimeter.

ASTM-F2656-2020.title: ASTM F2656/F2656M-20 Standard Test Method for Crash Testing of Vehicle Security Barriers
ASTM-F2656-2020.author: ASTM International
ASTM-F2656-2020.relevance_summary: The U.S. impact-test standard establishing M-rating (mass/speed) and P-rating (penetration) for perimeter and entry vehicle barriers. International equivalents: PAS 68 (BSI), IWA 14-1 (ISO).

CISA-HVM-2024.title: Vehicle Incident Prevention and Mitigation Security Guide
CISA-HVM-2024.author: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA)
CISA-HVM-2024.relevance_summary: Reference on vehicle-as-weapon attacks against crowded places and facility perimeters, with a Plan-Prevent-Protect framework and hostile-vehicle-mitigation barrier/bollard countermeasures.

CISA-SOFTTARGETS-2019.title: Security of Soft Targets and Crowded Places - Resource Guide
CISA-SOFTTARGETS-2019.author: U.S. Department of Homeland Security / CISA
CISA-SOFTTARGETS-2019.relevance_summary: Federal reference framework defining soft targets and crowded places (venues, houses of worship, malls) and protective measures against active-assailant, IED, UAS, and vehicle-ramming attacks.

RAND-SOFTTARGETS-2024.title: Improving the Security of Soft Targets and Crowded Places: A Landscape Assessment (RRA2260-1)
RAND-SOFTTARGETS-2024.author: Homeland Security Operational Analysis Center, RAND Corporation
RAND-SOFTTARGETS-2024.relevance_summary: Evidence-based landscape assessment of soft-target and crowded-place attacks: education and workplace buildings most frequently targeted; houses of worship, malls, and venues highest average lethality. Informs facility target-selection lethality weighting.

FBI-ACTIVESHOOTER-2024.title: Active Shooter Incidents in the United States in 2024
FBI-ACTIVESHOOTER-2024.author: Federal Bureau of Investigation / ALERRT Center, Texas State University
FBI-ACTIVESHOOTER-2024.relevance_summary: Categorizes every U.S. active-shooter incident by facility location type (commerce, education, government, houses of worship, healthcare, open space), giving the authoritative distribution of armed-assault attacks across facility categories.

NIOSH-BLDG-CBR-2002.title: Guidance for Protecting Building Environments from Airborne Chemical, Biological, or Radiological Attacks (DHHS/NIOSH Pub. 2002-139)
NIOSH-BLDG-CBR-2002.author: National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) / CDC
NIOSH-BLDG-CBR-2002.relevance_summary: The canonical U.S. government reference on HVAC and air-handling systems as a chemical/biological/radiological attack vector: ventilation/filtration hardening, physical security of air intakes, and airborne release inside buildings.

NIST-SP800-82-2023.title: Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security (NIST Special Publication 800-82 Revision 3)
NIST-SP800-82-2023.author: Stouffer, K., et al., National Institute of Standards and Technology
NIST-SP800-82-2023.relevance_summary: Authoritative federal standard for securing operational technology (OT/ICS/SCADA), explicitly covering building automation systems (BAS) and IT/OT convergence as an attack surface. Canonical for cyber-physical attacks on building controls.

GAO-15-6-2014.title: Federal Facility Cybersecurity: DHS and GSA Should Address Cyber Risk to Building and Access Control Systems (GAO-15-6)
GAO-15-6-2014.author: U.S. Government Accountability Office
GAO-15-6-2014.relevance_summary: Documents that building control systems (elevators, electrical, HVAC) and electronic access-control systems at ~9,000 federal facilities are internet-connected and vulnerable to cyber-attack, with a 74% rise in building/access-control cyber incidents FY2011-2014.

GAO-19-138-2018.title: Federal Building Security: Actions Needed to Help Achieve Vision for Secure, Interoperable Physical Access Control (GAO-19-138)
GAO-19-138-2018.author: U.S. Government Accountability Office
GAO-19-138-2018.relevance_summary: Focused treatment of Physical Access Control Systems (PACS) - card/reader/credential infrastructure - across federal buildings, including interoperability and oversight gaps exploitable in access-control compromise.

GAO-24-106744-2024.title: Critical Infrastructure Protection: EPA Urgently Needs a Strategy to Address Cybersecurity Risks to Water and Wastewater Systems (GAO-24-106744)
GAO-24-106744-2024.author: U.S. Government Accountability Office
GAO-24-106744-2024.relevance_summary: Assesses cyber vulnerability of ~170,000 U.S. water systems, naming unsafe drinking-water contamination as a consequence of operational-technology compromise. Bridges water-system security and contamination-via-systems-sabotage.

NAF-CLINICVIOLENCE-2024.title: NAF 2024 Violence & Disruption Statistics
NAF-CLINICVIOLENCE-2024.author: National Abortion Federation (NAF)
NAF-CLINICVIOLENCE-2024.relevance_summary: The definitive longitudinal dataset on ideologically motivated attacks against reproductive-health facilities since 1977: murders, bombings, ~200 arsons, clinic invasions, blockades and occupations. Core source for symbolic/ideological facility attacks and the occupation/blockade tactic.

CTC-INFRATERROR-2026.title: From Earth Liberation to Accelerationism: A High-Level Review of Fifty Years of Domestic Infrastructure Terrorism (CTC Sentinel 19:3)
CTC-INFRATERROR-2026.author: Humpal, J., Combating Terrorism Center at West Point
CTC-INFRATERROR-2026.relevance_summary: Original 194-incident dataset of extremist attacks and plots on U.S. critical-infrastructure facilities (1970-2025), tracing the shift from eco-sabotage arson to accelerationist electrical-grid and substation attacks. Recent scholarly source for symbolic/economic facility targeting.

USFA-ARSON-2021.title: Arson and Fire Investigation
USFA-ARSON-2021.author: U.S. Fire Administration (USFA), FEMA
USFA-ARSON-2021.relevance_summary: USFA national arson analysis and Topical Fire Report series covering motive categories, incendiary methods, and structure-fire arson trends. A second federal voice complementing NFPA and the ATF Arson Incident Report.

DHS-STCP-2018.title: Soft Targets and Crowded Places Security Plan Overview
DHS-STCP-2018.author: U.S. Department of Homeland Security
DHS-STCP-2018.relevance_summary: DHS's coordinated national approach to securing easily accessible, low-security public spaces (venues, schools, transit) against attack. Companion to the CISA Soft Targets Resource Guide.

CISA-CFATS-2023.title: Chemical Facility Anti-Terrorism Standards (CFATS)
CISA-CFATS-2023.author: U.S. Department of Homeland Security / CISA
CISA-CFATS-2023.relevance_summary: Chemical-facility security framework covering 300+ Chemicals of Interest and theft/diversion/release/sabotage security-issue categories. NOTE: statutory authority lapsed July 28, 2023 - cite as a historical/reference framework, not active regulation.

FBI-HOBAS-2024.title: Leveraging Data to Predict Outcomes in Hostage and Barricade Incidents (FBI HOBAS)
FBI-HOBAS-2024.author: Federal Bureau of Investigation, Law Enforcement Bulletin
FBI-HOBAS-2024.relevance_summary: Analysis drawing on the FBI Hostage Barricade Database System (HOBAS, 7,000+ incidents), the authoritative U.S. dataset for facility siege, barricade, and occupation incidents.

FBI-HATECRIME-2024.title: Hate Crime Statistics (Uniform Crime Reporting Program)
FBI-HATECRIME-2024.author: Federal Bureau of Investigation, UCR Program
FBI-HATECRIME-2024.relevance_summary: National anti-religious and bias-motivated crime data quantifying attacks on houses of worship and identity-associated facilities. Supports symbolic/ideological facility target selection.
